results.output: The box is a capable single-user drafting and summarisation tool that will not replace human review of client-facing work. At EUR 3,680 all-in, it delivers 92.28 tokens per second on the mixture-of-experts model, 28x real-time transcription, 93% accuracy on summarisation traps, and 91% correct tool selection with zero malformed calls. A LoRA adapter can be trained on the box itself with no cloud step, improving tone by 0.3 to 0.5 points. Three limitations matter for a ten-person practice. First, fine-tuning adapts voice but does not close the quality gap: local models scored 3.00 on send-readiness against 4.37 for the frontier cloud model, and the fine-tune did not move that figure. Second, the box serves one user at full speed at a time; simultaneous demand will queue or require a second unit. Third, on open-ended drafting the model will occasionally state a detail the source does not support, making human review of client-facing work mandatory rather than advisory.

Three findings from the evaluation warrant direct attention.

First, the fine-tuning exercise did not close the send-readiness gap. The local workhorse scored 3.00 on the independent grader's scale, while the frontier cloud model scored 4.37. After training a LoRA adapter on the box itself - two runs, 25 examples then approximately 100 - tone improved by 0.3 to 0.5 points, but faithfulness was unchanged and usability moved by 0.1 to 0.2, which sits inside the run-to-run noise band of 0.3 to 0.4. The adapter is a voice-adaptation tool, not a quality lever. A firm hoping to train away the need to edit will not get that from this hardware.

Second, the box serves one user at full speed at a time. When multiple people in the practice need output simultaneously, requests queue or a second unit is required. For a ten-person practice, this is a planning constraint, not a footnote.

Third, on open-ended drafting the local model will occasionally state a detail the source does not support. The 93% score on summarisation accuracy traps is strong, but it is not a guarantee. Human review of client-facing work is therefore mandatory, not advisory.

The box produces text at 92.28 tokens per second on its fastest model - roughly 70 words per second, so a full page of draft copy appears in under a minute. Its slower model manages 10.89 tokens per second, about 8 words per second, so the same page takes five times longer. Audio transcription runs at 28x real time, meaning a one-hour meeting recording is transcribed in about two minutes.

On document quality, the best local model scored 3.00 out of 5 on send-readiness, which means a professional would need moderate editing before filing or sending the work. The frontier cloud model scored 4.37 out of 5, meaning its output is close to send-ready with only light edits. That gap is the honest answer to your question: the local box is not yet as good as the big cloud assistants for drafting work you want to send without a second pass.

Where the local model does hold up well is accuracy. It scored 93% on summarisation accuracy traps, meaning it got 93 out of 100 tricky summary details right. It chose and called the correct tool in 91% of tasks with zero malformed calls, meaning it never produced a broken instruction.

The GMKtec EVO-X2 (EUR 3,680 all-in) delivers strong throughput - 92.28 tokens/sec on Qwen3-30B-A3B - and competent document work, with 93% summarisation accuracy and 91% correct tool calls. However, it does not close the send-readiness gap with frontier cloud models (3.00 vs 4.37), and fine-tuning on the box itself improved tone by only +0.3 to +0.5, which sits inside the noise band. It serves one user at full speed at a time, and human review of client-facing output remains mandatory.

The box costs EUR 3,680 as a cash outlay once Irish import VAT is counted. For a ten-person practice, that is a modest figure against the work it does. It runs a 30-billion-parameter model at 92.28 tokens per second on fresh context and transcribes audio at 28 times real time. A LoRA adapter was trained on the box itself with no cloud step, meaning client data never leaves the building.

The workhorse model scored 93% on summarisation accuracy traps and chose the correct tool in 91% of tasks with zero malformed calls. That is a reliable instrument for the daily work of drafting, summarising, and routing documents.

Three findings must be stated plainly. Fine-tuning improved tone by 0.3 to 0.5 points but did not close the send-readiness gap between local and frontier cloud models, which sits at 3.00 versus 4.37. This is a voice-adaptation tool, not a quality lever. A firm hoping to train away the need to edit will not get that from this hardware. The box serves one user at full speed at a time; heavy simultaneous demand queues or requires a second unit. On open-ended drafting the local model will occasionally state a detail the source does not support, so human review of client-facing work is mandatory, not advisory.

None of these findings is a reason to walk away. They are the terms of the arrangement.

A small firm that buys its own AI hardware - a mini PC with sufficient memory to run a local model - should expect three things. First, the transcription tool will process audio at 28 times real time, which is fast enough that a partner can listen to a client call and have a written summary before the next meeting. Second, the local model will select and call the correct tool in 91 per cent of tasks, with zero malformed calls, which means it can be trusted to route work through the firm's own systems without a human checking every step. Third, the cost is contained: EUR 3,680 as a cash outlay once Irish import VAT is counted, with no per-token fee accruing on every document the firm produces.

What the hardware will not do is close the quality gap with a frontier cloud model. On send-readiness, scored from one to five by an independent grader, the best local models score 3.00 against 4.37 for the cloud alternative. Fine-tuning on the box itself improves tone by 0.3 to 0.5 points but leaves faithfulness unchanged, and the usability gain of 0.1 to 0.2 sits inside the run-to-run noise band of 0.3 to 0.4. In practice, this means the local model is a voice-adaptation tool, not a quality lever. A firm hoping to train away the need to edit will not get that from this hardware.

One further limitation bears stating plainly. On open-ended drafting, the local model will occasionally state a detail the source does not support. Human review of client-facing work is therefore mandatory, not advisory.
